newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: INTERVIEW-Bangladesh sees higher economic growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Bangladesh sees higher economic growth.

text.p: Bangladesh expects to achieve higher economic growth in the new year starting in July by ushering in reforms and cutting government spending to spur investment, Finance Minister A.S.M.S Kibria said on Wednesday.

"We will try our best to maintain budgetary balance, reduce unnecessary government expenditure and increase private sector credit so that investment can take place to prop up the economy," Kibria told Reuters in an interview.
He said the government would continue to privatise state-owned industries and push through reforms in the banking sector and administration.
"The government will stimulate the economy by completing the reforms and by bringing about qualitative changes in the governance of the country," Kibria said
"Bureaucratic delay will be cut down...(and) decision making on the political level will be faster to bring dynamism into the administration."

The government was expected to set a target for gross domestic product (GDP) growth at 6.0 percent for fiscal 1997/98 beginning on July 1, following forecast growth of 5.7 percent for 1996/97, the minister said.

"We expect higher growth this year as Bangladesh's macro-economic situation is satisfactory. We had set the growth target at 5.5 percent for the year. Fortunately the rate will be more than 5.7 percent," he said.
GDP expanded by 4.7 percent in 1995/96 and 4.4 percent in the previous year.
On June 12, Kibria is expected to hand down the annual budget for the new year, the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's second budget since taking office in June 1996.
"We would continue to attract investment in industry and infrastructure. Our priority (for investment) is agriculture and human development," Kibria said.
"Agriculture is very important in our economy and a major contributor to the GDP. An overwhelming (majority of) our population is dependent on agriculture."
Bangladesh preferred not to give subsidies except for agriculture "if necessary", he added.
"It's a matter of food security for the people."

Kibria said Bangladesh's inflation rate was expected to remain below 4.0 percent by the end of 1996/97. "The rate of inflation was 3.17 percent in March and it will be definitely below 4.0 percent by the end of June," he said.

"This is an indication of a healthy economy. We will maintain our non-inflationery growth strategy. The government is very careful about the movement of prices for essentials and that it does not hurt the consumers."
"Responsible fiscal and monetary policies" should restrict inflation in the new year, Kibria said.
Bangladesh's foreign exchange reserves were expected to reach $2.2 billion by the middle of 1997/98, from $1.83 billion currently, he added.
"We have stabilised the country's foreign exchange reserves. It's now expected to rise to $2.2 billion by the middle of next year," he said.
